outline.chapter_title: Orientation: What DeepSeekMath Tries to Achieve
outline.description: Introduces the motivation, goals, and top-line results of DeepSeekMath. Sets expectations for what students will learn: building math-capable LLMs via large-scale math pretraining and efficient RL.
subtopics: The challenge of mathematical reasoning for LLMs
DeepSeekMath 7B at a glance: 51.7% MATH, 60.9% with self-consistency
Two pillars: high-quality math corpus and GRPO reinforcement learning
Positioning vs. GPT-4/Gemini and open-source landscape
Textbook roadmap and prerequisites

outline.chapter_title: Background: Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models
outline.description: Builds foundational knowledge on math reasoning with LLMs, key benchmarks, and prior approaches, equipping students to contextualize the paper’s contributions.
subtopics: Nature of math reasoning: symbolic, multi-step, verifiable
Benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, SAT, OCW, MMLU-STEM, BBH, CMATH, MGSM-zh, Gaokao variants
Prompting paradigms: chain-of-thought (CoT), program-of-thought (PoT), tool-integrated reasoning
Formal math and theorem proving: Isabelle, miniF2F
Prior models and corpora: Minerva, Llemma, OpenWebMath, Proof-Pile-2, MathPile

outline.chapter_title: Data Pipeline: Building the 120B-Token DeepSeekMath Corpus
outline.description: Details the iterative web-scale data mining process from Common Crawl and rigorous decontamination. Emphasizes methodology transferable to other domains.
subtopics: Seed corpus choice: OpenWebMath and rationale
FastText classifier training: positives/negatives, hyperparameters, iterations
Deduplication (URL and near-dup) and scale reduction
Domain-level mining and human-in-the-loop URL annotation
Iteration dynamics: coverage growth, stopping after diminishing returns
Decontamination protocol: n-gram exact matching against benchmarks
Multilingual collection: English and Chinese emphasis
Quality vs. volume trade-offs and selection thresholds

outline.description: Explains how the authors empirically validate the corpus vs. competing math corpora using controlled pretraining and downstream tasks.
subtopics: Controlled 1.3B-parameter experiments and training setup
Baselines: MathPile, OpenWebMath, Proof-Pile-2 (with Web/Code/arXiv mix)
Findings: higher average quality, steeper learning curves, longer scaling regime
Multilingual benefits and cross-lingual transfer (English↔Chinese)
Interpreting performance vs. tokens seen (avoid over-epoching small datasets)

outline.description: Covers initialization from a code model and the mixed data recipe that yields strong math and general reasoning performance.
subtopics: Initialization from DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B: why start with code
500B-token continual training mix: 56% DeepSeekMath, 4% AlgebraicStack, 10% arXiv, 20% GitHub code, 10% general CC
Optimization and scaling setup differences vs. 1.3B study
Evaluation without tools: CoT on GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, MMLU-STEM, Gaokao
Evaluation with tools: PoT on GSM8K and MATH
Formal math: autoformalization on miniF2F with Isabelle
General abilities: MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP
Key result: small but well-trained model rivaling or beating much larger models (e.g., Minerva 540B)

outline.description: Describes the curated SFT dataset and training protocol that align the base model for step-by-step and tool-integrated math solving.
subtopics: SFT dataset construction (776K examples): English and Chinese coverage
Solution formats: CoT, PoT, and tool-integrated reasoning
Training protocol: batching, context concatenation, hyperparameters
Comparative evaluation under no-tool and tool-allowed settings
Positioning vs. open- and closed-source instruction-tuned models

outline.chapter_title: From PPO to GRPO: A Practical RL Algorithm for Math Reasoning
outline.description: Teaches PPO in the LLM setting and introduces GRPO as a no-critic, group-relative variant that is cheaper and effective for math.
subtopics: Refresher on PPO for LLMs: actor-critic, KL regularization, advantage via GAE
Limitations in LLMs: value model overhead, sparse terminal rewards
GRPO concept: group-wise baseline via sampled outputs per question
Objective design: clipped ratio, KL regularization, unbiased KL estimator
Why group-relative aligns with preference-trained reward models
Compute/memory benefits from removing the critic

outline.chapter_title: GRPO Training Variants: Outcome, Process, and Iterative RL
outline.description: Walks through the practical GRPO variants used in the paper and when to use each to supervise math reasoning effectively.
subtopics: Outcome supervision: terminal normalized rewards per output
Process supervision: step-level rewards and cumulative advantages
Iterative RL: updating reward and reference models, replay with history
Algorithmic workflow: batching, sampling G outputs, updates per step
Hyperparameters that matter: group size G, KL coeff, clip range, LR

outline.description: Documents the GRPO run over math SFT data, and reports in-domain/out-of-domain impact, highlighting efficiency and generalization.
subtopics: RL data scope: CoT-format subsets of GSM8K and MATH (~144K Qs)
Reward model training data and initialization
GRPO settings: LR, KL coeff, group size (64), batch and length limits
Results: 88.2% GSM8K, 51.7% MATH without tools; gains on Chinese OOD
Self-consistency improvements; comparison vs. SFT-only Instruct
Ablations: online vs. offline, outcome vs. process supervision

outline.chapter_title: Unified Paradigm: SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, and GRPO as One Family
outline.description: Presents a single mathematical view to compare common post-training methods through data source, reward function, and algorithmic gradient coefficients.
subtopics: General objective form: data source, reward function, algorithm → gradient coefficients
SFT, RFT (offline), DPO, Online RFT (online), PPO/GRPO mappings
Key insight: online sampling outperforms offline as policy drifts
Why GRPO beats Online RFT: graded positive/negative coefficients
Process supervision advantages over outcome-only

outline.chapter_title: Empirical Insights: What Really Helped (and What Didn’t)
outline.description: Synthesizes the paper’s experimental lessons to guide practitioners on data and training design for math LLMs.
subtopics: Code training improves math reasoning (with and without tools)
Two-stage vs. one-stage mixes: catastrophic forgetting and mitigation
ArXiv pretraining appears ineffective for targeted math reasoning (with caveats)
Why RL works here: boosting robustness of output distribution (Maj@K vs. Pass@K)
Practical guidance on dataset diversity, multilinguality, and contamination control

outline.description: Provides a condensed, actionable blueprint to reproduce key components or adapt them to new domains (e.g., physics, finance).
subtopics: Data mining checklist: classifier bootstrapping, domain mining, human labeling
Corpus hygiene: dedup, decontam, multilingual balance
Training stacks: optimization schedules, batch sizes, context lengths
SFT recipe: format unification (CoT, PoT, tool integration), sampling and mixing
RL recipe: reward modeling (rule-derived labels → reward), GRPO default settings
Evaluation protocols: zero-/few-shot, CoT vs. PoT, self-consistency

outline.description: Honestly assesses gaps and risks, and charts research directions highlighted by the unified paradigm and findings.
subtopics: Current weaknesses: geometry, theorem-proving depth, few-shot limitations
Data bias risks and benchmark contamination safeguards
Scaling questions: model size vs. data quality vs. RL signal
Future RL: robust to reward noise, weak-to-strong, uncertainty-aware rewards
Data-side improvements: broader math domains, better multilingual coverage
Advanced sampling/decoding and efficient inference for exploration efficiency

outline.description: Concludes the textbook with a concise synthesis and a set of principles students can reuse when building domain-specialized reasoning LLMs.
subtopics: High-quality targeted pretraining can rival massive models
Start from code, add curated math, maintain general abilities
GRPO: simple, efficient, and effective for math RL
Unified view reduces algorithmic confusion and guides choices
Checklist for building strong open math LLMs
